scenes.synopsis: the copy-bringer, named — who brought the forgery to the stone; Creech, in the record.
scenes.prose:
> *(Creech is named fully — the Lantern's man of business, the proprietor's creature, the courier — and with the naming the chain stands complete before the jury like a rope laid out on a courtroom floor: the proprietor's hand to Creech's hand to the stone to the type to the town, each link sworn, each handoff witnessed, each step of the ruin's manufacture now a matter of record. Pettifer saw the handoff. He set the copy Creech brought. Creech carried it from the proprietor's desk with the proprietor's instruction — set special, lead the Thursday number, make it sing. The proprietor had it from a source, Creech said, and the word source hangs in the courtroom like a bad smell, because everyone present knows what it means: someone wrote it, someone paid for it, someone wanted it printed, and the Lantern asked no questions that might have gotten in the way of a Thursday number. The gallery's thin smile is the ton's particular expression — the pleasure of watching someone else's machinery exposed, the machinery they themselves wind every morning over chocolate. Quill lets the chain lie there, link by link, gleaming, and does not need to say what every person in the room is thinking: courier lines end at the hand that sent them. And the hand that sent this one sits twenty feet away, very still, watching his own rope being coiled. Rose thinks of the whisper-net, of the way the ton carries ruin from drawing room to drawing room with the same care Creech carried copy from desk to stone. The machinery is the same. Only the stationery differs. The chain lies on the courtroom floor, link by link, gleaming — and Quill does what great advocates do: he stops. He does not argue the chain. He does not decorate it. He lets it lie there, and lets the jury walk around it, and lets the gallery's whisper-net carry it bench to bench, because a chain this complete needs no counsel's voice. The proprietor's hand to Creech's hand. Creech's hand to the stone. The stone to the type. The type to the town — ten thousand breakfast tables, a hundred drawing rooms, a year's worth of ruin, all of it flowing from a source no one questioned and a hand no one checked. Rose watches the jury look at the chain, and then — inevitably, terribly — look at Pyke. By tomorrow, all of London will understand it.)*
> **Turns (8):**
> 1. [examine]Hear the full naming — "Mr. Creech," for the record. → Remembered: The go-between fixed in law; the chain has no missing link.
> 2. [micro]"After the stone was made up" — the lateness as evidence. → Remembered: Her grasp of the special handling; late copy means chosen copy.
> 3. [examine]"The proprietor had it from a source" — the gallery's thin smile. → Remembered: Her recognition of the gutter's favorite fiction; sources, invented.
> 4. [stance]Trace the chain — hand to hand to stone to town. → Remembered: Her courier-lines education, completed; every line ends at a hand.
> 5. [social]Watch "the chain close link by link." → Remembered: The methodical pleasure of completeness; she has learned to love evidence.
> 6. [examine]"Nowhere left for the lie to hide" — except the proprietor's mouth. → Remembered: Her anticipation of Pyke's stand; the mouth will open tomorrow.
> 7. [stance]Hold the season's parallel — ballrooms and stones, one craft. → Remembered: How she unites the season's two wars; tracing is tracing.
> 8. [choice]Mark Creech — pity, contempt, or use. → Remembered: What she intends for the go-between; the game keeps the intention.

scenes.synopsis: each libel, each invented source — undone, in the open; the unmaking begins.
scenes.prose:
> *(The unmaking begins, and its power is in how almost dull it is — no thunder, no revelation, just the slow, methodical, devastating work of truth applied to libel like a hot iron to a crease. The three libels are read aloud, one by one, in the clerk's flat, affectless voice, and each is met — not with rhetoric, not with passion, but with paper. The banker's ledger against swindled restoration: columns of figures, subscriptions recorded, wages paid, materials bought, every shilling of the restoration accounted for in ink that does not lie. The dated letters against duped suitors: a chronology laid out like a hand of cards, each suitor's arrival documented, each courtship conducted in the open, each honourable intention a matter of record. The solicitor's accounts against family fraud: the entail, the mortgages, the slow arithmetic of ruin faced and paid, creditors satisfied in order, the father's books closed clean. One by one the libels are emptied — their sources named, their claims measured, their type scattered — and the gallery gets what the ton so rarely gets: bookkeeping, as theatre. The fog burns off. The ton's embarrassment is a physical thing, a shifting in the benches, a sudden interest in gloves and programmes; Fane stops taking notes, which is the truest verdict the morning will produce. Truth, Rose thinks, watching the room turn, is plain bread — and the ton has been starving on cake. The libels were set in type. The ledgers were set in ink. Ink outlasts type, and everyone in the room knows it. The method of it is what undoes the ton — not thunder but bookkeeping, not revelation but arithmetic. Rose watches the gallery learn, in real time, what she learned over a year of ruin: that truth is slow and dull and devastating, and that lies are fast and glittering and fragile. The banker's ledger does not perform. It does not raise its voice. It simply states, column by column, that the restoration's money was recorded, receipted, accounted for — and the Lantern's swindle dissolves like fog in sun. The dated letters do not plead. They simply show, in chronological order, that the suitors came openly, courted honourably, and were never duped — and the Lantern's designing girl dissolves into dates. The solicitor's accounts do not protest. They simply prove, page by page, that the creditors were paid and the books closed clean — and the Lantern's family fraud dissolves into ink. The fog has burned off, and what stands in the clear air, white roses at her breast, is a lady the Lantern could not unmake — because she was never made of type to begin with.)*
> **Turns (8):**
> 1. [examine]Admire the dullness — "almost dull. That is its power." → Remembered: Her education in unmaking; boredom is a solvent for libel.
> 2. [micro]Hear each libel "read aloud in his flat advocate's voice." → Remembered: The advocate's instrument; flatness makes fog impossible.
> 3. [examine]Watch each source "named and then emptied." → Remembered: The anatomy of invention; nobodies, quoted as somebodies.
> 4. [social]Read the ton's embarrassment — "people who quoted these paragraphs at dinner." → Remembered: The gallery's complicity, exposed; diners become witnesses.
> 5. [stance]"Plain bread... killing the hunger" — savor the metaphor, or the fact. → Remembered: Whether she enjoys the unmaking; enjoyment has its own flavor.
> 6. [examine]Note Fane "stopped taking notes." → Remembered: The gossip's surrender, measured in a closed notebook; Fane's silence is a verdict.
> 7. [social]Feel the room "doing arithmetic." → Remembered: The jury's quiet labor; sums, not speeches, convict.
> 8. [choice]Let the dullness work, or wish for theatre. → Remembered: Her patience with process; the long game favors the patient.

scenes.synopsis: recess conference — the sequence of the unmaking; counsel and client take stock.
scenes.prose:
> *(At the second recess, in the corridor with its smell of damp wool and old paper, Mr. Quill reckons the morning's account with the satisfaction of a banker closing a sound ledger. Three libels down, he says — the forgery confessed, the copy traced, the claims undone by paper that does not lie — and the defense has not contested a word of it, which tells him everything about where the battle will actually be fought. Rooms follow paper, Rose says, and Quill's correction is gentle and devastating: Rooms follow whoever seems to be winning. The distinction matters, because the defense's play is now clear: it will not argue the letter was true. It will argue the Lantern believed it true — printed in good faith, on a source's word, and belief, the counsel will say, is not malice. The phrase sits between them again, that coin on the counter, and Rose turns it with a jeweller's care. What does the law do, she asks, to a paper that ruins by belief? Damages, Quill says. Costs. The public unmaking the ton is watching happen in real time. But Lavinia, scarlet and coiled at the corridor's end, wants more than damages — she wants destruction, the Lantern broken as an instrument, Pyke unmade as a proprietor, the whole sly machinery dismantled. A paper nobody believes, Rose says slowly, thinking of the morning's gallery, the ton's shifting benches, Fane's abandoned notebook — a paper nobody believes is only expensive kindling. Quill's smile is thin. Precisely. And kindling, Miss Hartwell, is what we are making. The corridor clock strikes. The afternoon belongs to the lady. They walk back into the courtroom together — counsel and client, the advocate and the lady — with the corridor's reckoning folded between them like a battle plan. The afternoon belongs to her: the telling, once, in daylight, the roof on Quill's architecture. Rose takes her place with Augusta's lesson running underneath everything like a bass note: lawyers mistake the weather for the climate. The room has turned today. The ton's favour is weather. But the record — the confession, the chain, the ledgers — the record is climate, and climate does not turn back. She looks at the witness box, empty and waiting, the cushion dented, the rail worn smooth, and feels the strangest calm: the general's calm, the calm of a woman who has prepared her ground and knows her artillery. Today the kindling gets its match.)*
> **Turns (7):**
> 1. [social]Take the smallest of smiles — Quill, permitting himself hope. → Remembered: Her reading of counsel's confidence; smiles are data.
> 2. [stance]"Rooms follow paper" — test her theory against his correction. → Remembered: Whether she revises the theory; winning, not paper, moves rooms.
> 3. [examine]Weigh "damages but not destruction." → Remembered: Her early measure of the possible victory; Lavinia's scale differs.
> 4. [social]Hold Lavinia's demand against the law's limits. → Remembered: The tension between ally and advocate; she stands between them.
> 5. [micro]"Expensive kindling" — carry the phrase like a picked flower. → Remembered: The image she keeps; kindling is its own kind of destruction.
> 6. [examine]Ask what the law can do — plainly, without varnish. → Remembered: Her insistence on plain answers; varnish is for gowns, not verdicts.
> 7. [choice]Return to the courtroom armed, or merely ready. → Remembered: The difference she draws; armed is a choice, ready is a state.

scenes.synopsis: the truth day's dress — white roses, worn; the gallery will read the wearing.
scenes.prose:
> *(The truth day's dress is a statement before she speaks a word, and Rose stands in Letitia's sitting room while the statement is assembled with the gravity of a military decoration. White roses — how worn, where worn, how many — is a grammar the ton reads before it reads testimony, and every choice is a sentence. At the breast: the declaration, open and unmissable, the clean name stated in cloth where the whole gallery can read it. In the hair: mercy, almost hidden, a softness the courtroom will not expect and the jury may remember. Carried, a single stem: prayer, or grief, or simply the habit of a woman who has learned that flowers say what the mouth cannot. Letitia's hands are steady and her mouth is full of pins, but her eyes are bright with an aunt's particular pride — the pride of a woman who has dressed a girl for a war and is watching her march. Augusta's note arrived with the roses: Wear it. You have earned the colour. Four words, underlined once, and Rose has read them three times. The ton will read the roses before they hear a word of testimony — the white throat to hem, the ivory thread, the Hartwell silver — and the reading will do half of Quill's work before he rises. Fashion is a courtship mechanic, and today the court being wooed wears wigs and sits in a jury box. She looks in the glass: the general, in white, roses at breast and hair and hand, the clean name made visible. Letitia steps back. The grammar is correct. The sentence is ready to be spoken. In the glass, the statement reads complete: white throat to hem, the ivory whitework catching the light, the Hartwell silver quiet at the wrist, the roses — breast, hair, hand — doing their silent work. Letitia steps back, pins spent, and Augusta's note lies on the dressing table like a commission: Wear it. You have earned the colour. Rose thinks of the season's long education in cloth — Élise's atelier, the rituals, the twenty pins and the five-coin decisions, the gowns that were arguments and the fittings that were strategy sessions. Every one of them was preparation for this: the day the cloth must testify. Fashion is a courtship mechanic, and today the court wears wigs. The cloth is telling the truth.)*
> **Turns (7):**
> 1. [choice]The roses at the breast — over the heart, found by every eye. → Remembered: Her choice of declaration; the clean name, worn where the heart is.
> 2. [choice]The roses in her hair — softer, half-hidden, found rather than shown. → Remembered: Her choice of mercy; the brief whispered, not stated.
> 3. [choice]A single rose, carried stem-down — like a lady going to church. → Remembered: Her choice of prayer; the brief stated once, then set aside.
> 4. [examine]Read Augusta's rescinded note — "wear it; you have earned the color." → Remembered: The general's permission, finally given; white is no longer withheld.
> 5. [social]Take Letitia's "dressmaker's gravity." → Remembered: The aunt's counsel in the retiring room; gravity suits the hour.
> 6. [stance]"Everything today is testimony" — dress as evidence. → Remembered: Her understanding that the wearing testifies; fashion is a courtship mechanic, even here.
> 7. [micro]Choose in the glass — the grammar of the wearing. → Remembered: Which grammar she speaks; the gallery will parse it before she speaks.

scenes.synopsis: the first libel undone — the "family fraud," refuted with the solicitor's accounts.
scenes.prose:
> *(The first libel is undone — family fraud — and the undoing is a masterclass in the difference between denial and refutation. The solicitor's accounts are produced, bound in red tape, and walked through page by page: the entail, with its iron arithmetic; the mortgages, taken in order and faced in order; the debts, listed to the shilling; the creditors, paid in the sequence the law requires and honour demands. Not denied — refuted. The distinction is the morning's whole philosophy, and Rose feels it land in the jury box like a stone dropped in still water: the Lantern claimed the Hartwells defrauded their creditors, and here are the creditors, paid, receipted, satisfied, their names read aloud like a roll of honour. The forged letter's wildest claim — that the family fortune was built on fraud — finds no entry in any column, no shadow in any ledger, no whisper in any account. A City juror nods, once, the small sharp nod of a man who trusts figures; the gallery is quiet with the particular quiet of people revising, in real time, a year's worth of dinner conversation. The ton had repeated family fraud over soup and fish with the confidence of the well-informed; now the well-informed are studying their gloves. Rose sits very still and lets the refutation do its work. She has learned, this season, that protest is noise and proof is music — and the courtroom is finally, after a year of type, hearing music. The first libel lies broken on the clerk's table, undone by ink that does not lie. The refutation settles over the courtroom like dust settling after a demolition — slow, complete, unarguable. Rose watches the jury absorb it: the City man's sharp nod, the foreman's careful note, the twelve faces doing the arithmetic of belief. They came expecting a lady's protest. They are getting a solicitor's accounts. The difference is the whole of Quill's strategy, and it is working like a well-oiled machine. In the gallery, the ton's revision is visible — the sudden interest in gloves, the averted eyes, the quiet conversations that will, by dinner, have rewritten a year's worth of certainty. We never believed it, they will say over soup. Not for a moment. The lie of it will be smooth and practiced and utterly ton. But the ledgers will not revise. The ledgers stand, bound in red tape, entered in ink, indifferent to drawing rooms. Not denied — refuted. And the lady in white sits very still, letting the refutation do what refutation does — outlast denial, outlive gossip, outstand everything but time itself.)*
> **Turns (8):**
> 1. [examine]Watch the foundation knocked out — "the rest wobbles." → Remembered: Her grasp of the case's architecture; foundations first, always.
> 2. [micro]"Columns that do not lie because columns cannot." → Remembered: Her faith in arithmetic over gossip; numbers simply stand.
> 3. [examine]Study the City juror's nod — "professional appreciation." → Remembered: Which juror is hers; the City man respects a clean ledger.
> 4. [social]Hear the gallery's quiet — "revising a month of dinner conversation." → Remembered: The ton's embarrassment, compounding; diners are revising.
> 5. [stance]"Not denied — refuted" — savor the distinction. → Remembered: Her preference for proof over protest; refutation outlasts denial.
> 6. [examine]"A lie leaves no ledger" — the sentence, kept. → Remembered: The maxim she takes from the morning; ledgers are lie-detectors.
> 7. [social]Note who looks away — the quoters, unmasked. → Remembered: Her catalogue of the embarrassed; the game keeps the names.
> 8. [choice]Feel triumph, or merely relief. → Remembered: Which emotion she permits; triumph flavors the Gazette's reading.

scenes.synopsis: the second libel undone — the suitors as dupes; dated letters, refuted.
scenes.prose:
> *(The second libel — duped suitors — collapses into dates, and there is something almost merciful in how cleanly it goes. The dated letters are produced in chronological order, laid out like a hand of winning cards: the suitors came with open eyes, each arrival documented, each courtship conducted in drawing rooms full of witnesses, each honourable intention a matter of record and correspondence. Quill calls no suitor to the stand — a decision of real elegance, Rose thinks, watching from the plaintiff's bench. Their conduct is its own testimony, he says, and the phrase does the work of ten witnesses: Julian's year of honourable patience, Laurent's careful neutrality, Henry's upright devotion — all of it conducted in the open, all of it witnessed by the ton itself, none of it duped and none of it duping. In the gallery, Julian does not flinch; Laurent's expression shifts by a fraction, the smallest possible acknowledgment; Henry sits like a standard planted in the ground. The story the Lantern told — a designing girl, a string of deceived men — dissolves into the dated, witnessed, documented truth: three honourable men, one honest woman, and a season of open courtship that half of London watched happen. Fane's notebook, which had reopened for the libels, closes again. The second libel joins the first on the clerk's table — undone not by rhetoric but by the calendar, which, unlike Fleet Street, keeps accurate time. The elegance of Quill's decision — to call no suitor — unfolds in the courtroom like a fan opening. Their conduct is its own testimony: the phrase does the work of ten witnesses, and Rose feels the suitors' silent testimony land in the jury box with the weight of honour itself. Julian, still as stone. Laurent, the fraction of acknowledgment. Henry, the planted standard. Three honourable men, one honest woman, a season of open courtship — the Lantern's designing girl dissolves, and what remains is the dated, witnessed, documented truth. In the gallery, the ton absorbs the lesson it most needed: that it watched this courtship happen, in its own drawing rooms, and chose to believe type over its own eyes. The embarrassment is exquisite and total. Fane's notebook closes — the arbiter declining to record what needs no recording. And Rose understands, with sudden clarity, why Quill called no suitor: to call them would have made it about men defending a woman. To not call them makes it about the truth defending itself. And the lady in white — who was never duped and never duping — sits in the clear air of dates that do not lie.)*
> **Turns (8):**
> 1. [examine]Watch the story die — "stories outlive paragraphs." → Remembered: Her understanding of narrative as the hardier libel; dates are the antidote.
> 2. [micro]Follow the chronological letters — each dated, each witnessed. → Remembered: The evidentiary power of order; chronology convicts.
> 3. [stance]"Their conduct is its own testimony" — receive Quill's delicacy. → Remembered: Her gratitude for the uncalled witnesses; honor, unexamined, stands taller.
> 4. [social]Read the three men — no flinch, a fraction, a standard. → Remembered: Each suitor's bearing under the gallery's eyes; the game keeps the readings.
> 5. [examine]"The romance was in the honor all along." → Remembered: Her reframing of the season's love stories; honor was always the plot.
> 6. [social]Note Fane's notebook, still closed. → Remembered: The gossip's continued silence; two closed notebooks make a pattern.
> 7. [stance]"The ton is learning to read" — permit the thought. → Remembered: Whether she allows herself the small triumph; permitted triumphs sustain.
> 8. [choice]Meet Julian's eyes, or keep her face to the court. → Remembered: Whom she acknowledges; acknowledgments are remembered by all parties.

scenes.synopsis: the third libel undone — the restoration as swindle; the banker's ledger, opened.
scenes.prose:
> *(The third libel — swindled restoration — meets the banker's ledger, and the meeting is not a contest. Page by page, column by column, the restoration's money is walked through before the jury: the subscriptions, recorded to the shilling; the payments to workmen, dated and receipted; the materials, invoiced and delivered; the wages, paid in order through the leanest months. A swindle does not usually keep receipts, Quill observes, in the driest tone of the day, and the gallery laughs — the sudden, surprised, genuine laugh of people who have been holding their breath and did not know it. The City juror's nod deepens; the foreman leans forward; even the judge's permanent patience seems to lighten by a degree. The Lantern's claim — that the restoration was a scheme, the subscriptions a fraud, the whole Hartwell revival a confidence trick set in type — lies exposed as what it always was: ink without accounts, accusation without arithmetic, a Thursday number built on a source and a grudge. Mrs. Bell's Gazette woman writes steadily through it all, her pencil never stopping, seventeen pages by Fane's later count, the only record of the day that will be set in honest type. Rose watches the ledger do its slow, devastating work and thinks of the mornings the ruin arrived with the chocolate — the ton reading swindle over breakfast, repeating it by luncheon, certain by dinner. Certainty, it turns out, is cheap. Receipts are expensive. And the Hartwells, whatever else the Lantern printed, kept their receipts. The laughter — sudden, surprised, genuine — does something to the courtroom that no argument could do: it breaks the spell. The ton has been holding its breath for a year, breathing the Lantern's fog, and Quill's dry observation — a swindle does not usually keep receipts — lets it exhale. Rose feels the room change in her bones: the gallery's shoulders dropping, the whisper-net dissolving into something almost like camaraderie, the shared relief of people who have been wrong together and are discovering it together. It is the most dangerous moment of the day, and the most hopeful — dangerous because the ton's favour is weather, hopeful because the weather has finally broken. Mrs Bell's Gazette woman writes through the laughter, steady as ever, seventeen pages and counting, the honest type being set in real time. The City juror's nod has deepened into something like conviction. The foreman is smiling — actually smiling, a thing foremen are not supposed to do. The Hartwells, whatever else the Lantern printed, kept their receipts — and receipts, it turns out, are the one thing type cannot counterfeit.)*
> **Turns (8):**
> 1. [examine]Watch the cleverest libel die — "the fraud's second act." → Remembered: Her defense of her proudest work; the Park's books are her armor.
> 2. [micro]"A swindle does not usually keep receipts." → Remembered: The line that broke the room; she'll quote Quill's mildness later.
> 3. [social]Hear the gallery's laugh — "the first real laugh of the day." → Remembered: The moment belief broke audibly; laughter is the libel's death rattle.
> 4. [stance]Feel the warmth — "laughing with the evidence, not at her." → Remembered: The distinction that steadies her; with, not at, is everything.
> 5. [examine]Note the City juror's deeper nod. → Remembered: The juror's growing allegiance; beautiful books persuade City men.
> 6. [social]Watch the Gazette's woman "write steadily." → Remembered: Her awareness of tonight's verdict being drafted; Bell scores steadily too.
> 7. [examine]"The restoration stands. The libel does not." → Remembered: The morning's epitaph, kept; she'll need it for the price, later.
> 8. [choice]Permit the warmth, or bank it for later. → Remembered: Whether she spends feeling mid-trial; banked warmth lasts longer.

scenes.synopsis: the room, turning — the ton's murmur, measured; the gutter weapon visibly spending itself.
scenes.prose:
> *(There is a moment — between the second libel's collapse and the third's — when Rose feels the gallery turn, and it is the strangest sensation of the day: not triumph, but weather changing. The silk-shift alters its pitch, the rising murmur of appetite giving way to something quieter, something almost like respect; the whisper-net, which has carried speculation from bench to bench all morning, falls silent, its carriers suddenly finding their gloves and programmes more interesting. Lord Fane closes his notebook and folds his hands — the gesture of a man who has come to record a hanging and found himself attending a vindication. The gutter's weapon is spending itself in the open, and a weapon spent in the open is only scrap. Rose understands, with a clarity that feels like cold water, what Augusta has been teaching her all season: you cannot push a room. You can only let it see, and wait, and be — in the seeing — the thing it cannot unsee. She has not performed. She has not pleaded. She has sat, in white, and let paper do what paper does when it is honest. Mrs. Bell's Gazette woman writes on, steady as a metronome, the honest type being set in real time. Lavinia, in her scarlet, is holding herself like a hound before the slip — the leash fraying, the year of patience nearly spent. And Pyke — Pyke's stillness has changed its character. It is no longer the coiled stillness of a spider. It is the stillness of a cornered thing, and the whole gallery can see it. The room has turned. The ton has turned. The only person in London who has not yet turned is the proprietor of the London Lantern, and his turn is coming. She lets the moment pass through her like weather — not grasping, not pushing, just being the thing the room cannot unsee. Augusta's lesson, learned over a season of drawing rooms: you cannot push a room. You can only let it see. And the room is seeing — the silk-shift's changed pitch, the whisper-net's silence, Fane's folded hands, the gutter's weapon spending itself in the open and becoming scrap. It is the strangest victory, this one: won by sitting still, in white, letting paper do what paper does when it is honest. No performance. No plea. Just the ledgers, the dates, the sworn accounts, and a lady who did not flinch. And the room — this room, which has learned to see — will be watching.)*
> **Turns (7):**
> 1. [examine]Date the turning — and fail; "turnings don't have timestamps." → Remembered: Her acceptance that victories arrive unannounced; she stops watching for them.
> 2. [social]Read Fane's closed notebook — "bellwether, barometer." → Remembered: The ton's weather vane, folded hands; when Fane stops writing, the town has decided.
> 3. [stance]"You cannot push a room" — Augusta's lesson, applied. → Remembered: Her discipline of non-interference; light does the pushing.
> 4. [examine]Study Pyke's stillness — "no longer coiled. Cornered." → Remembered: The flavor-change in the enemy; cornered is different from coiled.
> 5. [social]Note Lavinia "holding herself... before the slip." → Remembered: The ally's leashed hunger; the hound waits for the slip.
> 6. [micro]Sit "very still" and let it happen. → Remembered: Her mastery of stillness as action; stillness, done right, is testimony.
> 7. [choice]Touch the turning, or let it turn untouched. → Remembered: Whether she reaches for the moment; untouched turnings hold longer.

scenes.synopsis: called to the stand — the ruin, about to be retold true; the box, at last.
scenes.prose:
> *(She is called to the stand, and the courtroom inhales — one body, one breath, the ton's collective anticipation made audible. Rose rises and walks the general's walk: measured, unhurried, the white roses at her breast uncrushed, her eyes on the witness box and not on the gallery, because a general does not survey the crowd before the guns begin. The oath she takes looking at the judge, not at the room — her voice clear, her hand steady on the book, the words falling like stones into still water. Quill is gentle with her, as he was gentle with Pettifer — the gentleness of a man who knows that the truth, properly handled, needs no force — and the questions come soft: the family, the ruin, what the Lantern printed and what the world actually did. She tells it the way she has decided to tell it — not performing, not surviving, simply stating, the way a ledger states. The entail. The mortgages. The father's death and the books closed clean. The forged letter, a practiced imitation of a hand she knew better than her own. The restoration, beam by beam, receipt by receipt. She does not embroider. She does not plead. She tells it once, in daylight, and then she will never tell it again — and the courtroom, which has heard a year of type, hears at last a human voice, steady and unadorned, saying what happened. The white roses do not tremble. Her voice does not tremble. Somewhere in the gallery, Lavinia makes a small sound — not a sob, never a sob, but the sound of a held breath finally released. The walk to the witness box is the longest walk of the season — longer than any ballroom entrance, longer than the Vauxhall steps, longer than the mornings she walked into drawing rooms knowing what the Lantern had printed. The courtroom inhales. The gallery leans. The white roses do not tremble. She takes the oath looking at the judge — her voice clear, her hand steady — and the words fall like stones into still water: the truth, the whole truth, nothing but the truth. Quill's questions come soft, the surgeon's gentleness, and she answers the way she decided in the corridor: plainly, once, in daylight. The entail. The mortgages. The father's death. The books closed clean. The forged letter — the practiced imitation of a hand she knew better than her own. And the courtroom, which has heard a year of type, hears at last the thing type could never counterfeit: a human voice, steady and unadorned, telling the truth once, in daylight, and then — forever — never again.)*
> **Turns (8):**
> 1. [micro]Walk "the general's walk, unhurried, unbowed." → Remembered: The gait the season taught her; the box receives a general.
> 2. [stance]Take the oath "looking at the judge, not the gallery." → Remembered: Her hierarchy of regard; law over weather, always.
> 3. [social]Receive Quill's gentleness — "handled like a fright." → Remembered: Whether she accepts the compliment; frights are allowed truth.
> 4. [examine]Distinguish telling from performing, from surviving. → Remembered: Her naming of the act; telling is the one thing left undone.
> 5. [micro]Hear the courtroom inhale — "the thing courtrooms do." → Remembered: The room's anticipation, registered; inhales precede verdicts.
> 6. [social]Feel Lavinia "a held breath." → Remembered: The ally's suspense; even scarlet holds its breath.
> 7. [examine]Hear the small clear voice — "once, in daylight, and then never again." → Remembered: The private vow beneath the oath; it will govern the telling.
> 8. [choice]Open her mouth — as plaintiff, daughter, or witness. → Remembered: Which self testifies first; the box remembers.

scenes.synopsis: the retelling — the ruin retold true, in daylight; fraud, refuted, in her own voice.
scenes.prose:
> *(The retelling holds the room the way a held note holds a concert hall — complete, unbroken, the silence around it part of the music. She tells it in the order she chose in the corridor: the Hartwell fortune first, the entail and the mortgages and the slow arithmetic of ruin faced honestly; the creditors paid in order, the father's death, the books closed clean and the name left honest — and here she pauses, because the pause is where the jury will live, in the space after honest. Then the Lantern's letter: a practiced imitation, common ink, a worn crease, a hand she knew better than her own set in type as if type were truth. Then the restoration — beam by beam, subscription by subscription, the workmen paid through the lean months, the receipts kept because her father taught her that ink outlasts gossip. She does not embroider. She does not raise her voice. She does not look at Pyke, or at the suitors, or at the gallery — she looks at the jury, twelve men, and tells them what happened, once, in daylight. No, she says, when Quill asks whether any of the Lantern's claims were true. Nothing. It was set in type. It was not set in truth. The sentence lands like a hammer on an anvil. Fane writes three words in his notebook and underlines them twice. The courtroom does not breathe. And Rose, who has told it once, in daylight, feels the telling leave her like a breath held for a year — and does not pick it up again. The silence after the telling is the fullest silence of the trial — the held note, the concert hall, the room understanding that it has witnessed something that cannot be repeated. Fane's three words, underlined twice, stand in his notebook like a monument. The jury sits very still — twelve men who came expecting a lady's protest and got a ledger's music instead. And Rose, stepping down, feels the telling leave her like a breath held for a year: the entail, the mortgages, the father's hand, the imitation, the restoration — all of it spoken, once, in daylight, into the record where no type can touch it. It is done. She will never tell it again. The vow settles over her like a cloak: the ruin has had its daylight, and daylight is done with it. And the truth — stated once, never to be repeated — stands in the record like a stone.)*
> **Turns (8):**
> 1. [examine]Tell it "in the order she chose" — the architecture, inhabited. → Remembered: Her ownership of the telling's shape; chosen orders hold.
> 2. [micro]Pause at "his name honest" — the pause as testimony. → Remembered: The silence inside the sentence; pauses convict better than adjectives.
> 3. [social]Describe her father's hand — "a daughter's knowledge." → Remembered: The intimacy deployed as evidence; love, stated plainly, is proof.
> 4. [stance]"She does not embroider. She does not perform. She states." → Remembered: The register of the retelling; stating outlasts performing.
> 5. [examine]Hear the pen "sound like weather." → Remembered: Her awareness of being scored mid-sentence; Bell's pen is weather.
> 6. [social]"Nothing. It was set in type. It was not set in truth." → Remembered: The line the town will quote; type versus truth becomes the season's epitaph.
> 7. [examine]Watch Fane write three words. → Remembered: The gossip's verdict, in triplicate brevity; three words can be a whole judgment.
> 8. [choice]Finish — and let the silence stand, or fill it. → Remembered: Whether she trusts the silence; finished tellings need no coda.

scenes.synopsis: cross-examination — Pyke's counsel probes; she holds the line, in white, in daylight.
scenes.prose:
> *(The cross-examination is a duel fought with fans instead of swords, and Pyke's counsel is good — sly, quiet, reasonable, every question a barb wrapped in silk. Was the entail quite so simple as she describes? Were the creditors truly paid in the order she claims? Did she know her father's hand so well — so very well — that she could swear to an imitation? Each question is a small blade, slipped between the ribs of her testimony, and the courtroom watches to see if the lady bleeds. She does not. She answers plainly, briefly, without ornament — yes, no, that is correct, I have said what happened — and the very plainness becomes a kind of armour, because there is nothing for the barbs to catch on. When the counsel probes the suitors — those honourable gentlemen, their intentions, their understanding — she gives the smallest possible smile, the one Augusta taught her, and says: Ask them. The gallery laughs — sudden, genuine, delighted — and the counsel, to his credit, does not press. He is sly, not stupid, and he can read a room. She steps down with the white roses uncrushed, the general's walk carrying her back to the plaintiff's bench, and the courtroom exhales. Once, in daylight, and never again — the telling is done, the testimony given, the truth set in the record where no type can touch it. Lavinia's eyes are bright. Quill's nod is the smallest possible benediction. And Pyke's counsel sits down, his silk-wrapped barbs spent, having drawn no blood from a woman who came to court dressed in white and armed with receipts. The counsel sits down, his silk-wrapped barbs spent, and the courtroom understands what it has witnessed: a duel fought with fans, and the lady undefeated. Rose returns to the plaintiff's bench with the general's walk, the white roses uncrushed, and feels the room's regard like sunlight — warm, complete, the ton's favour at last aligned with the truth. It is weather, she reminds herself, Augusta's lesson running underneath the warmth. Weather changes. But today — today the weather is fair, and she permits herself to feel it: the gallery's delighted laugh still ringing, Lavinia's bright eyes, Quill's thin approving smile, the jury's attentive faces. She answered plainly. She answered briefly. She gave the barbs nothing to catch on. Ask them — the smallest smile, the two words that undid an hour of sly questioning. The cross-examination is over. The testimony stands. You cannot make a woman bleed who came to court dressed in white and armed with receipts.)*
> **Turns (8):**
> 1. [examine]Grant him "good" — the enemy's counsel, assessed. → Remembered: Her fairness to adversaries; granted competence is its own confidence.
> 2. [micro]Feel each question — "barbs folded inside like blades in a fan." → Remembered: Her reading of sly examination; fans open both ways.
> 3. [stance]Answer "plainly, briefly, without ornament." → Remembered: Augusta's discipline, deployed; plainness is armor under cross.
> 4. [examine]"Ask them" — the smallest of smiles, the gallery's laugh. → Remembered: The moment the cross broke; smiles under fire win juries.
> 5. [social]Hear the laugh — the room, with her. → Remembered: The audible turning; laughter under cross is a verdict's preview.
> 6. [stance]Step down "with the roses uncrushed." → Remembered: The ritual's survival of examination; uncrushed roses testify.
> 7. [examine]"Once, in daylight, and never again" — the line, intact. → Remembered: Her keeping of the private vow; kept vows compound.
> 8. [choice]Meet Pyke's eyes on the way down, or don't. → Remembered: Whether she looks at the proprietor; looks are remembered by proprietors.

scenes.synopsis: the general's verdict on the day — Augusta, in the corridor, scores her granddaughter.
scenes.prose:
> *(In the corridor afterwards, Augusta is waiting, and for once the general's composure has a crack in it — not weakness, but the particular brightness of a woman who has watched her work come right. Well, Augusta says, and the single word carries a campaign's worth of meaning. You told it. I told it once, Rose says. In daylight. The corridor is crowded with the ton dispersing, silk rustling, voices rising, the whole glittering machinery of London society reassembling itself around the day's events — and the two women stand in the middle of it like rocks in a stream, unmoved and unmovable. Rooms turn when the paper does, Rose says, thinking of the gallery's changed pitch, Fane's closed notebook, the City juror's nod. Quill is a lawyer, Augusta says, with the dryness of long experience. Lawyers mistake the weather for the climate. The correction lands gently and stays: the room turned today, but rooms turn back; the ton's favour is weather, and weather changes. What does not change — what cannot unprint itself — is the record: the testimony given, the ledgers entered, the confession sworn. Whatever the jury does tomorrow, Augusta says, and her voice drops to the register she uses for things that matter, you told it. Once. In daylight. No one can unprint that. Rose thinks of Lavinia's note, the four words in her reticule: Broken, darling. Not bought. Watch. The watching is done. The telling is done. What remains is the verdict — and the verdict, whatever it is, will find a woman who has already won the only victory that cannot be taken: she spoke, in the open, and the truth stayed spoken. They stand in the corridor's stream like rocks — the general and the lady, the aunt and the niece, the two women who held the household together through the ruin's worst mornings. Around them the ton disperses, silk rustling, voices rising, the war's machinery standing down for the day. Rose thinks of the morning's note, still in her reticule: Broken, darling. Not bought. Watch. The watching is done. The telling is done. What remains is the verdict — and the rope, and Pyke's stand, and the morrow's last page. But Augusta is right, and the rightness settles over her like evening: whatever the jury does tomorrow, she told it. Once. In daylight. No one can unprint that. But today — today the lady told it, and the telling stands, and no one, not even Fleet Street, can unprint the daylight.)*
> **Turns (8):**
> 1. [social]Receive "Well" — "a campaign's worth of assessment." → Remembered: How she takes the general's commendation; stated facts are Augusta's medals.
> 2. [examine]"Lawyers mistake the weather for the climate." → Remembered: The sentence she keeps; Augusta's maxims outlast counsel's.
> 3. [stance]Walk "the general's pace" beside her. → Remembered: The inherited gait, finally shared; grandmothers transmit through walking.
> 4. [social]Hear "no one can unprint that" — the truth's permanence. → Remembered: Her grasp of what the day secured; told truth is un-unprintable.
> 5. [micro]Carry the words "like a second set of seams." → Remembered: The general's blessing, worn under white; seams hold.
> 6. [examine]"The verdict that matters may already be given." → Remembered: Her private reckoning; some verdicts precede juries.
> 7. [stance]Almost laugh — "the most Augusta sentence ever uttered." → Remembered: The laughter she permits mid-war; grandmothers are good for morale.
> 8. [choice]Tell Augusta about the vow — "once, in daylight" — or keep it. → Remembered: Whether the private vow goes shared; shared vows gain witnesses.

scenes.synopsis: ★ KEY DECISION 2/3 — PETTIFER'S FATE. The confessed man's future, weighed in the corridor; mercy and law both have their price. (Turns: 3 — the decision)
scenes.prose:
> *(Pettifer has confessed before the ton — the small hours, the stone, the copy set special, the hand he knew was wrong and set anyway — and the law, having heard him, wants its due: suborning a forgery and setting it known-false is a hanging matter in the statute's cold eye, whatever the courtroom's warm sympathy. Quill lays the fates like cards in the corridor: mercy — spare the decent man in the fright, let the confession stand as its own punishment; Law — the full weight, the statute's price, because the ton must see that ruin-by-type has a cost; purse — the practical middle, a fine and a kept silence, the man's livelihood spared and the lesson priced. Lavinia wants the severe — she has waited a year, and mercy feels like softness, and softness feels like the ruin winning. But the man unmade himself honestly before the whole ton, and honesty, Rose thinks, is the rarest thing the trial has produced — rarer than ledgers, rarer than confessions bought and paid for. The statute is cold. The courtroom was warm. Somewhere between the two lies the fate of a frightened compositor.*
*★ KEY DECISION 2/3 — Pettifer's fate:*
- **Mercy, openly** — *Gazette flavor set: merciful.* Spare him publicly; the confession stands as its own punishment.
- **The law, fully** — *Gazette flavor set: severe.* The statute's price; ruin-by-type must be seen to cost.
- **Fine and silence** — *Gazette flavor set: practical.* A priced lesson, the man's livelihood spared.
> *(The game remembers the choice — and the means: the open mercy, the severe law, or the practical purse. The destination was never in doubt. The signature is hers.)*

scenes.synopsis: the defense — Pyke's counsel's last effort; the gutter's case, spent before the room.
scenes.prose:
> *(The defense rises, and the courtroom learns what sly looks like in a wig: Pyke's counsel does not contest the forgery — does not dare, with Pettifer's confession still warm in the record — but builds, instead, a cathedral out of belief. The Lantern printed in good faith, he argues, on a source's word; a newspaper is not a court, and cannot try every letter before it sets it; to punish a proprietor for believing is to punish all of Fleet Street, and where then would the ton read its mornings? Belief isn't malice, he says, laying the phrase on the counter like a coin, and the courtroom turns it over. It is thin, but it is not nothing — the City man's brow furrows, the foreman's pencil pauses, and Rose feels the room's weather shift by a degree. Then Quill rises, and with a single question demolishes the cathedral: if the Lantern merely believed, why did the proprietor's own man carry the copy to the stone with instructions to set it special — to lead the Thursday number, to make it sing? A proprietor who believes does not need his forgery set special. The counsel has no answer — the silence stretches, the gallery leans, and the defense's whole edifice settles, audibly, into the mud. The summing continues, but the heart has gone out of it; the argument exits the courtroom sounding like what it is — an excuse, dressed in a wig, billing by the hour. Rose watches Pyke's face through the collapse, and the stillness is still there, but it has thinned, like ice in March. Belief isn't malice. But special setting is not belief. And the jury has heard both. The defense's cathedral settles into the mud, and the courtroom watches it sink with the particular satisfaction of people who enjoy seeing clever men outwitted. Rose studies Pyke through the collapse — the stillness thinned like March ice, the calculation visible underneath, the man doing the arithmetic of his own unmaking in real time. He does not look at his counsel. He does not look at the jury. He looks at the record — the chapel's confession, the chain's links, the ledgers' columns — the way a man looks at a tide coming in. Belief isn't malice: the coin on the counter, the phrase his counsel laid so carefully. But Quill's single question — why set it special? The morrow waits.)*
> **Turns (8):**
> 1. [examine]Hear the defense — "what a gutter press sounds like." → Remembered: Her assessment of the enemy's voice; gutters can't sing.
> 2. [micro]"Belief isn't malice" — "like a coin on a counter." → Remembered: Her test of the phrase's ring; counterfeit rings hollow.
> 3. [stance]Watch the jury — "it is not nothing." → Remembered: Her honesty about the defense's weight; thin can still cut.
> 4. [examine]Note the City man's frown — "at his columns." → Remembered: Which juror wavers; the City man needs one more sum.
> 5. [social]Hear Quill's single question — "set special." → Remembered: The reply's architecture; one question can be a whole closing.
> 6. [stance]Feel the stillness — "the counsel has no answer." → Remembered: The moment the defense died audibly; stillness is the sound.
> 7. [examine]"An excuse" — name what the defense became. → Remembered: Her final classification; excuses don't win juries.
> 8. [choice]Savor it, or stay braced. → Remembered: Whether she permits premature triumph; braced women last longer.

scenes.synopsis: the forged letter, broken up — the sort, scattered; the lie, unmade into metal.
scenes.prose:
> *(In the corridor after the court rises, with the judge's permission and before witnesses, Pettifer takes the forme and breaks it up — and the ton, which came for a hanging, gets instead the day's truest theatre. The quoins are loosened, the chase opened, the locked lines of type lifted from the stone one by one; the compositor's hands, ink still in the cuticles, move with the reverence of a priest unmaking a sacrament. It is only metal now, Pettifer says, so quietly that only the nearest hear — and the nearest carry it outward, bench to bench, the whisper-net running in reverse, carrying truth for once instead of ruin. The sort is scattered into the type case, each letter finding its compartment, the ruin unmade the way it was made: by hands, one letter at a time — only this time the hands are honest, and the scattering is witnessed, and no one will ever set that forme again. Lavinia makes a small sound — not triumph, something rawer, the sound of a year of patience finding its end. Rose watches the letters fall — the L of Lantern, the H of Hartwell, the whole alphabet of a year's ruin dissolving into compartments — and thinks of the mornings the paper arrived with the chocolate, the ton reading destruction over breakfast. It was set in type. Now it is scattered in type. The difference between ruin and justice, it turns out, is the direction the letters travel: into the forme, or out of it. It is not a hanging. It is an unprinting. And the unprinting is done. The letters fall — the L of Lantern, the H of Hartwell, the whole alphabet of a year's ruin — each finding its compartment in the type case with a small, final click. Pettifer's hands move steadily, the compositor's reverence unbroken, unmaking the forme the way he made it: one letter at a time. The witnesses watch — the clerk, the counsel, the ton's representatives — and the unmaking is formal, witnessed, complete. It is only metal now. The sentence, spoken so quietly, carries to the back of the corridor: the ruin, reduced to its elements, sorted into compartments, never to be set again. Rose thinks of the mornings — a year of mornings — the paper arriving with the chocolate, the ton reading destruction over breakfast. It was set in type. Now it is scattered in type. The type will never set that ruin again.)*
> **Turns (7):**
> 1. [examine]Watch the quoins loosened — the unprinting, literal. → Remembered: Her witnessing of the lie's disassembly; she was present at the unmaking.
> 2. [micro]See "the lie dissolving into the alphabet." → Remembered: The image she keeps; lies are only letters, misarranged.
> 3. [stance]"It's only metal now" — receive Pettifer's epitaph. → Remembered: The workman's sentence; metal, unlike lies, can be melted for honest work.
> 4. [social]Hear Lavinia's small sound — "not quite a laugh, not quite a sob." → Remembered: The ally's emotion, leaking; even scarlet cracks at unmakings.
> 5. [examine]"Unmade the way it was made" — by hands, one letter at a time. → Remembered: Her understanding of symmetry; ruins and unruins share a method.
> 6. [stance]"This time the hands were honest" — mark the difference. → Remembered: The moral of the type case; honesty is a manual trade.
> 7. [choice]Stay to the last letter, or leave at the scattering. → Remembered: Whether she witnesses completely; complete witnesses remember completely.

scenes.synopsis: the ally watches her revenge ripen — broken, not bought; the hunger, and the line.
scenes.prose:
> *(In the carriage going home, Lavinia comes apart by degrees — not weeping, never weeping, but the scarlet gloves twisted white-knuckled in her lap, the year's patience finally showing its cost. Did you see his face, she demands. When Quill asked about the special setting — did you see it? I saw the room, Rose says, because the room is what matters and they both know it. But Lavinia is past strategy now, past the ally's cool counsel, down to the wound underneath the weapon: a year, she says. A year of watching him print and print and print, of smiling at his dinner table while he set my friend in type like a — like a notice of auction. And now — is it enough? The damages, the costs, the public unmaking — is it broken, Rose? Tell me you see it breaking. The carriage rattles over cobbles; London slides past, grey and indifferent. Rose looks at her ally — her dangerous, devoted, half-ruined ally — and chooses her words the way Élise chooses thread: Broken, she says, not bought. And not broken by cruelty — broken by completeness. By ledgers and dates and confessions, by the whole dull devastating weight of truth applied like a hot iron. Call it justice, if you like. Lavinia's breathing slows. The gloves untwist, finger by finger. Justice, she repeats, tasting the word. It is not the word she came in with — she came in with revenge — but it is the word she leaves with, and the leash, frayed all day, holds for one more night. Watch, she says softly. And Rose, watching, thinks: the watching is nearly done. The carriage rattles on, London sliding past grey and indifferent, and the two allies sit in the treaty-silence of women who have said what needed saying. Rose thinks of the year's strange mathematics: the Crane name spent in rooms where it will not be forgotten, the threats absorbed before they could land, the men paid to come to London and tell the truth — all of it Lavinia's doing, all of it the ally's agenda made manifest. She wants Pyke broken. She has never pretended otherwise. And Rose — Rose wants the clean name, the record set straight, the ruin unprinted. The wants overlap. They have always overlapped. That is what makes the alliance work, and what makes it dangerous. Broken, not bought, Rose repeats, tasting her own verdict. And the leash — frayed all day, tested all day — holds for one more night.)*
> **Turns (8):**
> 1. [social]"Did you see his face?" — revenge, savored. → Remembered: How she answers the ally's savoring; she redirects toward the room.
> 2. [examine]See the white-knuckled scarlet gloves. → Remembered: The ally's cost, visible in her hands; revenge has a grip.
> 3. [stance]"The room's the verdict" — correct the aim, gently. → Remembered: Her insistence on the open victory; verdicts, not faces, are the prize.
> 4. [social]Hear "a stone in her shoe" — the year-long carrying. → Remembered: Her new measure of Lavinia's wound; stones in shoes shape walks.
> 5. [examine]"Not by cruelty. That was the line." — restate the boundary. → Remembered: Her restatement of the line; lines restated hold firmer.
> 6. [stance]"By completeness" — accept the amendment, or refuse it. → Remembered: Whether completeness passes as justice; amendments need watching.
> 7. [micro]Feel the fraying leash — "the ally's hunger is a hound." → Remembered: Her sense of the alliance's strain; hounds pull, leashes fray.
> 8. [choice]Hold the leash tighter, or let it run. → Remembered: Her handling of Lavinia's hunger; the eve will test the grip.

scenes.synopsis: the room, turned — the ton watches the gutter weapon spent; the clean name, voted in real time.
scenes.prose:
> *(The evening calls come unbidden — three countesses, a bishop's wife, Fane without his notebook — and Rose receives them in the drawing room with the white roses still fresh at her breast, because the day is not done being won. They talk of the trial the way the ton talks of weather that has broken: with relief, with revision, with the particular amnesia of people who were never, not for a moment, on the wrong side. We never believed it, the eldest countess says, over tea. Not for a moment. The lie is so smooth, so practiced, so utterly ton, that Rose almost admires it — this is the weather changing in real time, the climate of opinion shifting while the tea cools. Fane, notebookless, stays an hour and talks of everything except the trial, which is his way of saying everything about it; he mentions, in passing, that Mrs. Bell's Gazette woman took seventeen pages, and the number hangs in the air like a verdict. Letitia pours. Augusta presides. The white roses do their silent work. And Rose understands, with the clarity of the utterly vindicated, what the day has actually won: not the jury's verdict — that comes tomorrow, or the next day — but the room's. The ton tried her in its drawing rooms all evening, and acquitted her without a dissenting voice. No one can unprint what the room saw today: the ledgers, the dates, the lady in white telling it once, in daylight. She won in the open, without buying a verdict, without spending a favour, without bending a single rule. The calls go on till ten. When the door closes on the last of them, Letitia says: Well. And Augusta says: Indeed. And that, in the Hartwell house, is triumph. The last call goes at ten — Fane, lingering over the final cup, notebookless and almost human — and the door closes on the ton's acquittal with a soft, final click. Letitia sinks into her chair with the particular exhaustion of generals after a successful campaign. Augusta reviews the evening like a battle report: three countesses, a bishop's wife, Almack's Wednesday secured, Fane's hour of deliberate not-talking-about-it. Well, she says. Indeed, says Letitia. And Rose — Rose stands at the window with the white roses still at her breast, looking out at the square's lamplit grey, thinking of the day's strange double victory. But tonight — tonight the house is quiet, the roses are wilting gently, and the peace sounds exactly like a drawing room at ten o'clock.)*
> **Turns (8):**
> 1. [social]Receive the unbidden calls — "the ton invited itself." → Remembered: Her reading of the social signal; unbidden calls are votes.
> 2. [examine]"We never believed it" — the ton's lie, decoded. → Remembered: Her fluency in drawing-room fiction; decided lies are still decisions.
> 3. [micro]Note Fane's "conspicuously absent" notebook. → Remembered: The gossip's disarmament, performed; absent notebooks are white flags.
> 4. [social]Hear "seventeen pages" — the Gazette's appetite. → Remembered: The scale of Bell's interest; seventeen pages means a verdict is coming.
> 5. [stance]Receive them "in white, with the roses still fresh." → Remembered: The ritual's endurance into evening; fresh roses testify all day.
> 6. [examine]"Without buying the verdict, without owning the judge." → Remembered: Her naming of the victory's terms; the open win is the whole season.
> 7. [social]Watch the embarrassment — "misjudged the forecast." → Remembered: The ton's weather, revised; forecasters revise quietly.
> 8. [choice]Accept the lie graciously, or mark it. → Remembered: Whether she lets the ton's fiction stand; gracious winners are quoted kindly.

scenes.synopsis: Quill's closing — the gutter weapon, named and spent, before the jury.
scenes.prose:
> *(The next morning Mr. Quill closes, and the closing is the roof going onto the architecture he raised on the first day — no new timber, no ornament, just the final beams laid with the same craftsman's care. He does not raise his voice. He does not need to. He walks the jury through it, step by step, the way a man walks a friend through a house he has built: the letter, confessed by the hands that set it; the copy, carried by the proprietor's own man with instructions to set it special; the libels, undone one by one by ledger and date and sworn account; the lady, who told it once, in daylight, and asked for nothing but to be heard. And then the turn — the quiet, devastating turn: what, he asks, does Fleet Street become, if a proprietor may do this? If belief is a shield for special setting, if a source is a licence for forgery, if the ton's mornings may be poisoned with impunity? The judge sums up with weary fairness, the jury is charged, and the courtroom holds its breath — and then the ripple, the silk-shift of pure appetite: before the jury retires, the plaintiff will call the proprietor. Ambrose Pyke will take the stand. The announcement lands like a stone in still water. The jury has heard the chapel confess, the copy named, the libels undone, the lady tell — and now, before deliberation, it will hear the man himself, the hand behind the type, the mouth behind the libels. There is nowhere left for the lie to hide, Rose thinks, watching Pyke's stillness go very, very quiet — nowhere left except his own mouth. And his mouth, tomorrow, will have to open. The judge's charge is weary and fair — the permanent judicial patience applied, one last time, to the evidence: the confession, the chain, the ledgers, the lady. The jury listens with the particular attention of men who know they are about to decide something. And then Quill's announcement — the plaintiff will call the proprietor — lands like a stone in still water, and the courtroom's breath catches. Ambrose Pyke will take the stand. The ripple goes through the gallery — silk-shift, whisper-net, Fane's pencil racing — and Rose feels the day's architecture find its final beam. They have heard the chapel confess. They have heard the copy named. They have heard the libels undone and the lady tell. And I — I have told it once, in daylight, and I am done.)*
> **Turns (8):**
> 1. [examine]Hear the architecture finished — "the roof on the building." → Remembered: Her sense of the case's completeness; roofs make buildings habitable.
> 2. [micro]"What Fleet Street becomes if he may." → Remembered: The question Quill leaves hanging; juries answer hanging questions.
> 3. [stance]"The gutter's last stand, and you are the wall." → Remembered: Her translation of the mildness; mild advocates build walls.
> 4. [social]Feel the ripple — "the proprietor will be heard." → Remembered: The gallery's appetite for the final act; ripples precede storms.
> 5. [examine]"Nowhere left for the lie to hide except his own mouth." → Remembered: Her anticipation, sharpened; mouths are the last refuge of lies.
> 6. [stance]Sit "very still" through the closing. → Remembered: Her discipline at the climax; stillness, again, as testimony.
> 7. [social]Note the judge's "weary fairness." → Remembered: Her read on the bench; weariness can be fairness's mask, or its face.
> 8. [choice]Think of the scattered sort — comfort, or omen. → Remembered: Which image she carries forward; alphabets await their mouth.

scenes.synopsis: the odds, reckoned — counsel's honest assessment before the proprietor's stand.
scenes.prose:
> *(In the corridor, with the jury not yet retired and Pyke's summons still warm in the air, Mr. Quill reckons the odds with a candour he affords to no one but his client. He will be sly, Quill says. The soul of reason. He never threatened anyone — that much is true, and the truth of it is his armour. All his cruelty was in the type, and type can be disowned with a shrug. The performance of innocence, Quill calls it, and the phrase is exact: Pyke will take the stand and be reasonable, and the reasonableness will be the threat. The cross-examination is the question now — who holds the rope, and how hard to pull. Quill lays the options like cards: he does it, all counsel's craft and no lady's emotion; she does it, the plaintiff herself, the woman Pyke ruined, asking the questions herself; or they decline, let the record speak, trust the chapel and the copy and the ledgers to hang him without another word. His own men unmake him, Rose says slowly, thinking of Pettifer's hands scattering the type, of Creech's name spoken aloud, of the chain laid link by link. The record is a rope, Quill agrees. But someone must hold the other end. In the corridor's end, Lavinia waits in scarlet, the leash fraying visibly now, a year of patience down to its last threads — and Rose knows what her ally wants: not counsel's craft, not the record's slow rope, but the lady herself, the ruined woman, asking the questions with a steady voice and white roses at her breast. Broken, darling, Lavinia mouths across the corridor. Not bought. Rose nods. The decision waits for the morrow. The rope waits for a hand. The corridor empties slowly — the ton dispersing, the counsel gathering papers, the clerk locking doors — and Rose stands with Quill in the fading light, the decision between them like an unsheathed blade. His own men unmake him: the phrase has the ring of strategy and the weight of truth. Pettifer confessed. Creech was named. The type was broken up before witnesses. The record is a rope, coiled and ready — but ropes, Quill reminds her, do not hang men by themselves. Someone must hold the other end. She thinks of the options laid like cards: his craft, her voice, the record left to speak. And the lady — who told it once, in daylight — waits for the morning, white roses ready, the general's calm settled over her like armour.)*
> **Turns (8):**
> 1. [social]Hear the refrain — "tired of it the way you're tired of true things." → Remembered: Her fatigue with accurate warnings; true things weary too.
> 2. [examine]"His cruelty was all in the type." → Remembered: Her final understanding of Pyke; type was always the weapon.
> 3. [stance]"A performance of innocence" — preview the enemy's theatre. → Remembered: Her preparation for the performance; forewarned juries watch harder.
> 4. [examine]Weigh the three crosses — his, hers, or none. → Remembered: Her tactical assessment; the choice approaches.
> 5. [social]"His own men unmake him" — the phrase, kept. → Remembered: The strategy's kernel; unmaking by one's own is the cleanest.
> 6. [micro]Think of "Lavinia's leash, fraying." → Remembered: The ally's hunger, present even here; leashes fray fastest near prey.
> 7. [stance]Hold the line — "not broken by cruelty." → Remembered: Her boundary, rehearsed; lines hold if they're held early.
> 8. [choice]Ask Quill what he would do, or decide alone. → Remembered: Whether counsel's counsel sways her; the decision is hers regardless.

scenes.synopsis: Julian in the gallery — the last secret's keeper, watching; trust, holding.
scenes.prose:
> *(In the corridor afterwards, Julian finds her — or she finds him; in the crowded aftermath of a trial day, finding is mutual — and for a moment the year's careful choreography drops away. He exhales, and the sound is a man setting down a weight he has carried for twelve months: You told it well, he says. Once. In daylight. The corridor is full of the ton dispersing, silk and voices and the clatter of the war's machinery standing down, but the two of them stand in an eddy of quiet, the way they stood at Vauxhall when everything changed. I have been listening all season, he says, and the simplicity of it undoes something in her chest — this honourable man, this patient man, who spent the season's secrets and strained its trust and never once asked for more than she could give. The secret is spent now, the Vauxhall confession a matter of record between them; what remains is the map — the Network's London interests, the banking-house threads and shipping lines he has spent a year charting, the last guess he has held back. After the verdict, he says. When it is yours to use. The timing is his final courtesy: not now, not in the heat of vindication, but after, when the weapon can be wielded coolly. After, she agrees, and the word is a promise and a postponement at once. He bows — the old bow, the honourable bow — and is gone into the crowd. Rose stands in the corridor with the white roses at her breast and thinks: the trial unmakes the past. The map unmakes the future. And Julian, patient Julian, has given her both the weapon and the wisdom to wait. He is gone into the crowd — the old bow, the honourable bow — and Rose stands in the corridor's eddy with the encounter settling over her like dust. A year, she thinks. A year of Julian's patience: the Vauxhall confession, the secrets spent, the trust strained and holding, the map being drawn in quiet rooms while the ton watched the trial. The Network's London interests — banking-house threads, shipping lines, the men who move money for the faceless principal — charted by an honourable man for an honourable purpose, held back until the moment it could be used coolly. After the verdict. When it is yours to use. And the trial — which unmakes the past — rolls toward its verdict, while the map — which unmakes the future — waits, folded, for the day it will be hers to use.)*
> **Turns (8):**
> 1. [social]"Unclear who finds whom" — the pattern, noted. → Remembered: The nature of their meetings; some people orbit, mutually.
> 2. [examine]See the exhale — "holding his breath for a year." → Remembered: Her recognition of his relief; exhaling men are honest men.
> 3. [stance]"You told it well. Once. In daylight." — receive his verdict. → Remembered: How his approval lands; the coerced man's praise is freely given.
> 4. [social]Feel the crowded corridor — "so much unsaid." → Remembered: The weight of the unspoken; trust carries what words can't.
> 5. [examine]"The last guess, given freely" — the map, offered. → Remembered: The gift's terms; freely given beats coerced, always.
> 6. [stance]"After the verdict. When it's yours to use." — accept the timing. → Remembered: Her patience with the gift; maps keep.
> 7. [micro]"His fear, spent" — name what the offering costs him. → Remembered: Her tenderness toward the cost; spent fear is its own courage.
> 8. [choice]"After," she agrees — or asks for it now. → Remembered: Whether she takes the map early; after is a promise, now is a demand.

scenes.synopsis: ★ KEY DECISION 3/3 — PYKE'S STAND. Who holds the rope when the proprietor testifies; the cross-examination's hand, chosen before the morrow. (Turns: 3 — the decision)
scenes.prose:
> *(Pyke takes the stand tomorrow — the soul of reason, the soul of Fleet Street, sly and never overt — and the cross-examination's hand must be chosen tonight. Quill lays it out in the robing-room with a candour he affords no one but his client: he does it, all counsel's craft, the record's rope pulled by professional hands; she does it, the plaintiff herself, the woman Pyke ruined, asking the questions with a steady voice and white roses at her breast; or they decline, let the chapel and the copy and the ledgers hang him without another word, the rope left unheld. Lavinia wants her — the leash fraying, the year's patience down to its last threads, the ally's whole hunger in four words: broken, darling, not bought. He will be reasonable, Quill warns, and the reasonableness will be the threat. Every answer true and none of them honest — thirty years of Fleet Street craft in every syllable, the belief that shields, the source that cannot be named, the special setting explained as a proprietor's natural interest in his Thursday number. The record is a rope, and ropes do not need the hanged man's cooperation. But someone must hold the other end, and the hand that holds it will be remembered longer than the verdict.*
*★ KEY DECISION 3/3 — Pyke's stand:*
- **She crosses him herself** — *Gazette flavor set: plaintiff.* The ruined woman asks the questions; the ton watches.
- **Quill crosses him** — *Gazette flavor set: counsel.* Professional hands pull the record's rope.
- **Decline the cross** — *Gazette flavor set: record.* Let the chapel, the copy, and the ledgers hang him.
> *(The game remembers the choice — and the means: her own voice, her counsel's craft, or the rope left unheld. The destination was never in doubt. The signature is hers.)*

scenes.synopsis: the gambit announced — the proprietor will be called; the gallery's ripple.
scenes.prose:
> *(The third morning, and the courtroom is a theatre before the last act — every seat taken, the gallery packed to the doors, the ton having scented an ending and come to witness it the way it witnesses everything: thoroughly, fashionably, and with lunch ordered for afterwards. Mr. Quill rises, and his announcement is the flint on the steel: the plaintiff will call the proprietor. Ambrose Pyke will take the stand. The ripple goes through the room like wind through wheat — the silk-shift of pure appetite, the whisper-net igniting bench to bench, Fane's pencil poised over a fresh page. They have watched the chapel confess and the copy-bringer named; they have watched the libels undone one by one, ledger by ledger; they have watched the lady tell it once, in daylight. Now they will watch the man himself — the hand behind the type, the mouth behind the libels, the proprietor of the London Lantern, called to account in the open. Pyke's stillness, through the announcement, does not break; but there is a flicker at the corner of his mouth, there and gone, and Rose reads it the way she has learned to read him: calculation, not fear. He will be the soul of reason. He will never have threatened anyone. He will print his innocence the way he printed her ruin — sly, smooth, and utterly without a threat anyone could swear to. The clerk prepares the oath. The witness box waits, its cushion dented, its rail worn smooth. A rope, Quill said. And tomorrow, everyone in the room understands, someone will hold the other end. The ton has scented an ending, and there is nothing — nothing in all of London — like the ton scenting an ending. Every seat taken. The gallery packed to the doors. Fane with a fresh notebook, the Gazette's woman with her pencil poised, the suitors in their scattered positions, Lavinia's scarlet visible from the street. Rose sits in white among them — the plaintiff, the lady, the one they have watched all season — and feels the theatre's particular electricity: the held breath before the last act, the audience knowing the ending and needing to witness it anyway. Quill's announcement is the flint on steel. The plaintiff will call the proprietor. The ripple goes through the room like wind through wheat. And tomorrow — tomorrow the soul of reason takes the stand, and the record, patient and complete, will be waiting.)*
